article_title: Practitioner's Guide to Integrating Literacy and Science
citation: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Nine-lesson phenomenon-driven sequence: introduce phenomenon, observe, question, experiment, share data, read, revise model, extend
description: The guide sketches a nine-lesson sequence (approximately 45 minutes each) driven by a single phenomenon: why some playground surfaces are hotter than others. Students read an engaging narrative, record initial ideas in journals, make playground observations, narrow a testable question, design and conduct experiments, share and argue over data, read with a need to know, revise a class consensus model, and design engineering solutions. The guide notes "the entire set of lessons are driven by the single phenomenon."
requirements: A puzzling everyday phenomenon that can be explained if students master the focal science concepts
constraints: Lessons 1-3 are appropriate for grades K-6; Lessons 4-9 are most appropriate for grades 3-6
The sequence takes place over nine lessons of approximately 45 minutes each, daily or across weeks
target_learning_goals: Explaining a scientific phenomenon (Sun's effect on Earth's surface)
Authentic reading, writing, and scientific discourse
examples: Students touch surfaces or use infrared thermometers to observe temperature patterns, then design poster-board color experiments.
key_sources: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/practitioners-guide-to-integrating-literacy-and-science/

article_title: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report
citation: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Four-level phonological awareness progression from rhymes and syllables to phoneme manipulation
description: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency structures its Phonological Awareness domain as a research-based developmental progression "with two measures at each of four levels": Level 1 Rhymes and Syllables, Level 2 Syllable Blending and Initial Sounds (a transitional level), Level 3 Phoneme Blending and Segmenting, and Level 4 Syllable and Phoneme Manipulation. Reports also include a Level 0, indicating readiness for Level 1 concepts, and a Level 5, indicating Level 4 concepts can be reinforced. Within-domain adaptivity selects measures based on student performance within this progression.
requirements: Adaptive selection of a subset of measures within the progression during each test event
constraints: Level 2 is transitional, indicating whether students are ready to move on to phoneme blending and segmentation
target_learners: Pre-K through grade 2 students developing Spanish phonological awareness
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness skills supporting decoding, aligned to CCSS en español foundational skills standards
examples: Rhyme Completion and Counting Syllables at Level 1; Phoneme Substitution and Syllable Addition/Deletion at Level 4, each with printed item specifications and CCSS en español alignments
key_sources: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/

article_title: Next Generation Science Standards in Practice: Tools and Processes Used by the California NGSS Early Implementers
citation: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Phenomena-based, three-dimensional conceptual flow for mapping a multi-week NGSS unit storyline
description: The conceptual flow is "a process for graphically mapping the storyline of a three-dimensional (3D) NGSS instructional unit lasting six to eight weeks or longer", carried out collaboratively by same-grade teachers in five steps: identify an anchor phenomenon, individually pre-think needed concepts, create a collaborative cluster map, match SEPs, DCIs, and CCCs to the grade level, and sequence concepts into a coherent graphic. The graphic differs from a concept map by also showing the hierarchy of ideas and the sequence for instruction, and serves as a reference for planning the learning sequences within the unit.
requirements: Collaborative development through conversation with colleagues; the report states much of the value resides in the collaborative experience rather than the product alone
constraints: Development is time-intensive; conceptual flows are often modified over time with a mindset of continuous improvement
target_learners: K-8 students; the pattern is used by teachers of grades K-8
target_learning_goals: Coherent, student-centered NGSS unit design integrating science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and crosscutting concepts
examples: A Grade 5 conceptual flow for the unit "What's in Our Water?" with the anchor phenomenon that sewage water can be made drinkable, connected investigative phenomena, CCCs, SEPs, and DCIs, with each column representing a learning sequence
key_sources: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596757

article_title: Exploring How Agent Voice Accents Shape Human-AI Collaboration in K-12 Group Learning
citation: Ravi, P., Stevens, C., Hurt, B., Hanks, B., Lin, G., and Anderson, E. (2026). Exploring How Agent Voice Accents Shape Human-AI Collaboration in K-12 Group Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12805
title: Phoenix: a voice-based, non-embodied LLM conversational peer agent for group learning
description: Phoenix is a "voice-based, non-embodied conversational agent that joins real-time group discussions through spoken dialogue with multiple participants", positioned as an equal peer supporting knowledge co-construction rather than an authoritative tutor. Its architecture integrates Google speech-to-text, Microsoft Azure text-to-speech, and OpenAI's GPT-4.1-mini on a Django backend, with a GPT-4.1-mini-based gatekeeping classifier analyzing the eight most recent dialogue turns to decide when Phoenix should respond. Phoenix was implemented with Indian, British, and African American accents while keeping the LLM prompt and tasks constant.
requirements: Runs on a shared laptop at the group table with a web interface displaying spoken output alongside a live transcript
A gatekeeping classifier that analyzes the eight most recent dialogue turns to determine when the agent should respond
The LLM generating responses is not informed of the synthesized accent type, to prevent accent-related cultural biases in outputs
constraints: Designed for one-off, lab-based workshop interactions in this study rather than longitudinal classroom use
Technical constraints, including latency and limited model transparency, affected interaction flow and trust
target_learners: K-12 teachers in small-group problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: Collaborative problem-solving and consensus building
Equitable, human-led participation in group discussion
examples: In the study, 33 teachers in 11 groups of three interacted with Phoenix across an icebreaker, a survival-task consensus activity, and an open-ended brainstorming task, with accents varied between groups via Azure voices Arjun, Bella, and Lola with pitch adjustments for gender neutrality

article_title: Meeting Urban and Rural District Needs for Educators: California State University, Bakersfield's Teacher Residencies
citation: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823
title: Phase-in schedule pacing resident responsibility and Danielson Clusters across the residency year
description: A reusable program-level design in which the clinical year is broken into 2-week increments that specify residents' coteaching roles, responsibilities, and strategies, plus focal Danielson Clusters that coursework reinforces in the same period. As printed, "These schedules broke each semester into 2-week increments and advised mentor teachers and residents about the roles, responsibilities, and coteaching strategies they should consider taking on during each period." Clusters are paced so residents cycle through all six once in fall and again in spring, reinforcing learning across semesters.
requirements: Mentor teachers able to shift the timeline based on their assessment of resident readiness
Course instructors who align coursework to the focal Cluster for each period
constraints: Mentor teachers may adjust the phase-in timeline according to resident readiness, so pacing is advisory rather than fixed
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates in yearlong clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of teaching practice across the Danielson Framework Clusters
examples: Scheduled observations focused on the Cluster named for the period, with written feedback shared at weekly Coaching Time and with program coordinators

article_title: Design and Implementation of a Real-time Multi-site Immersive Learning System Using Photon Fusion
citation: Iwai Wataru, Duc V . Nguyen. (2026). Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Multi-Site Immersive Learning System Using Photon Fusion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10325
title: Photon Fusion-based multi-site VR immersive learning system with real-time voice and shared 3D materials
description: A VR learning environment in which teachers and students connect via Wi-Fi using VR headsets and communicate through Photon Cloud, which acts as a central server to synchronize object states and audio among all clients in real time. Voice communication integrates Photon Fusion with Photon Voice 2, initiated when a client enters the VR classroom. Learning materials include 3D chemistry apparatus, e.g. a flask containing Calcium hypochlorite and a pipette containing hydrochloric acid, with chlorine gas rendered as yellow-green smoke that bleaches blue litmus paper.
requirements: Participants connect to the Internet via Wi-Fi using a VR headset (Meta Quest 3 in the reported use)
constraints: The prior peer-to-peer system it replaces supported only up to five people; the new system is designed for twenty participants
target_learning_goals: science experiment learning, e.g. three-dimensional understanding of chemistry phenomena
examples: A science lesson in which manipulating a pipette generates chlorine gas rendered as yellow-green smoke, bleaching blue litmus paper

article_title: Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning
citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Interpret physiological predictions within broader context; never use them as standalone decision-making tools
description: The article's ethics section recommends that predictions of academic performance derived from physiological data be treated as one input among many rather than as autonomous decision tools. It states that such predictions "should be interpreted within the context of other influential factors, such as personal circumstances, environmental conditions, and mental health considerations, to guarantee fairness and mitigate biases." High-stakes decisions such as educational interventions must incorporate these insights within a broader context to avoid imposing undue stress and unintended consequences on students.
requirements: Use of publicly accessible datasets and fully documented computational methodologies, including model parameters and hyperparameters, to promote reproducibility; averaging findings over multiple runs
constraints: Predictions are not intended to stand alone as decision-making tools; high-stakes decisions must incorporate broader context
target_learners: college students in high-stress exam settings
target_learning_goals: supporting student well-being and mental health awareness alongside academic performance monitoring
examples: The article suggests educators, mental health professionals, and stakeholders can leverage the study's framework to build stress-monitoring and performance-prediction tools that uphold ethical standards
key_sources: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960

article_title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: PhysicsMate benchmark of 1,834 curriculum-grounded Bengali physics QA pairs
description: PhysicsMate is a benchmark of 1,834 question-answer pairs derived from the official NCTB Grade 9-10 physics textbook (13 chapters, 359 pages), written in formal Bengali. Each pair is "linked to a specific knowledge node and originating semantic unit", giving curricular provenance back to textbook passages. The corpus is partitioned into training (n = 1,374; 74.9%), validation (n = 185; 10.1%) and held-out test (n = 275; 15.0%) sets, stratified by chapter, with programmatic checks that no question ID appears in more than one partition. The benchmark and knowledge graph are released with a Dataset Card.
requirements: Each benchmark item must be grounded in a specific NCTB textbook passage kept as metadata, so answers use the source curriculum's terminology, formulas and unit conventions.
constraints: The benchmark covers a single national curriculum, NCTB Grade 9-10 physics, and generalization to other syllabi or subjects has not been tested.
target_learners: Grade 9-10 secondary physics students in Bengali-medium education
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned secondary physics question answering in Bengali
examples: Chapter 1 (Physical Quantities and Measurement) contributes the most items (302), while Chapter 12 (Magnetic Effects of Current) contributes the fewest (82).
key_sources: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664

article_title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: Multi-relational knowledge graph of the NCTB physics syllabus with ten ontological node types
description: The knowledge graph formalizes the 13-chapter NCTB syllabus as a multi-relational structure with 1,760 nodes across 10 ontological types (concepts, questions, quantities, figures, examples, entities, definitions, formulas, laws, HSC topics) and 2,600 directed edges spanning 30 relation types. Relations include curricular hierarchy (part_of), applicability (applies_to), visual grounding (illustrates), example relations (example_of), dependency (depends_on) and provenance (derived_from). The graph serves as "a structured curricular index of the source material" used for category-level analysis, with every node traceable to source textbook pages.
requirements: Extraction uses a predefined domain ontology and a fixed structured prompt so equivalent curricular facts receive consistent representation, and each record retains source-page provenance.
constraints: The 10-node ontology maps directly to STEM domains; non-STEM or humanities curricula would require restructuring the declarative and procedural primitives into causal, temporal and narrative relation types.
target_learners: Grade 9-10 secondary physics students in Bengali-medium education
target_learning_goals: Structured curricular knowledge representation enabling category-level evaluation of physics QA
examples: Table I reports node counts per type, e.g. 397 concepts, 224 quantities, 83 formulas and 65 laws.

article_title: RoboBuddy in the Classroom: Exploring LLM-Powered Social Robots for Storytelling in Learning and Integration Activities
citation: Tozadore, D., Ertug, N., Chaker, Y., & Abderrahim, M. (2025). RoboBuddy in the Classroom: Exploring LLM-Powered Social Robots for Storytelling in Learning and Integration Activities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16706
title: PhinetunEd: a Phi-3 model fine-tuned for educational content creation
description: PhinetunEd is the authors' name for a Phi-3-Mini-128k-instruct model (3.8B parameters, 128K context window) fine-tuned with QLoRA on a consumer GPU using 2500 samples from Cosmopedia, a synthetic dataset of educational resources including story-generation instruction tasks. It was built because of "concerns about data privacy and the need for improved performance in pedagogical tasks" and runs on a laptop without an internet connection, keeping data locally processed and stored. In benchmarks it scored best of the compared models on story generation (7.46) while scoring below GPT-3.5-turbo on MMLU and Hellaswag.
requirements: Fine-tuning used QLoRA with quantization and low-rank adapters to fit a consumer GPU
constraints: The authors considered only small language models of around 3 billion parameters or fewer due to limited computing resources and the need for timely responses
target_learning_goals: story generation and Q&A creation from curriculum content
examples: Teachers shown outputs from both models said GPT stories could be more engaging while PhinetunEd provided more room for teacher intervention to dive deeper into concepts

citation: Yossi Ben-Zion, Roi Einhorn Zarzecki, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein. (2024). Leveraging AI for Rapid Generation of Physics Simulations in Education: Building Your Own Virtual Lab. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07482
title: Reusable prompt template specifying animation, sliders, buttons, graphs, and responsive layout
description: The article provides a general prompt template instructing the LLM to act as a web developer creating an interactive simulation with "A real-time animation of the system", "Sliders to adjust system parameters", start/pause/reset buttons, time-series graphs of relevant quantities, and responsive design. The template is flexible enough to be customized for different physical systems such as Mechanics or Electricity and Magnetism.

article_title: A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI
citation: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522
title: Philosophical tradition: critical thinking as reflective judgment, dialogue, lived experience, and critique of power, inspiring critical and speculative design in HCI
description: The review presents critical thinking as a broader philosophical orientation concerned with cultivating reflective judgment, questioning taken-for-granted assumptions, and articulating values, informed by pragmatism, dialogic perspectives, phenomenology, and critical theory. It notes that "In HCI, this has inspired critical and speculative design, feminist HCI, and value-sensitive design", approaches that make visible the values systems embody and create openings for users to question technologies.
requirements: Communicating context-specific criteria (laws, regulations, norms, or ideals) used for judgment is essential in this tradition
constraints: This tradition treats critical thinking as partly political, oriented toward transforming the conditions in which technologies are designed and used, not only analysis
target_learners: HCI researchers and designers; users of computational systems
target_learning_goals: Reflective judgment; questioning assumptions; articulating values; critique of technological mediation
examples: The review traces pragmatist inquiry from Peirce, James, and Dewey through Schön's reflective practitioner into research-through-design in HCI
key_sources: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522

article_title: Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Yvonne M. Fromm (2026). Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102394
title: Feedback as a phase-sensitive mechanism within SRL cycles
description: The article theorizes adaptive feedback not as a uniform external input but as a mechanism whose function depends on where in the SRL cycle it is taken up. Building on the self-regulation process model (Schmitz & Wiese, 2006), it links directive feedback to translating forethought into regulatory behavior, informative feedback to monitoring and calibration during reflection, and transformative feedback to connecting post-actional reflection to subsequent forethought, while stressing these alignments are not exclusive to one phase. The study "provides a basis for theorizing feedback as a phase-sensitive mechanism within SRL cycles, rather than as a uniform external input."
requirements: Feedback uptake must be linked to phase-specific SRL appraisals to determine when different feedback functions apply
constraints: The article's own results showed moderating effects were limited and inconsistent, so the mechanism's benefits are conditional rather than uniform
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across pre-actional, actional, and post-actional phases
examples: In studybuddy, strategy videos operationalized directive feedback, the dashboard informative feedback, and combined use transformative feedback, with uptake recorded weekly from log files
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Yvonne M. Fromm (2026). Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102394

article_title: Effects of physical activity on executive functions, attention and academic performance in preadolescent children: a meta-analysis
citation: de Greeff, J. W., Bosker, R. J., Oosterlaan, J., Visscher, C., & Hartman, E. (2018). Effects of physical activity on executive functions, attention and academic performance in preadolescent children: a meta-analysis. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 21(5), 501-507. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2017.09.595
title: Subdomain taxonomy for physical activity effects: four executive function, three attention and three academic performance subdomains
description: The meta-analysis organises its outcome measures into a taxonomy of cognitive and academic subdomains: "Four subdomains of executive functions (inhibition, working memory, cognitive flexibility and planning), three subdomains of attention (selective, divided and sustained) and three subdomains of academic performance (mathematics, spelling and reading) were distinguished." This structure lets intervention effects be quantified separately per subdomain and by study design, activity type and intervention duration. It frames how the reviewed intervention studies' outcomes were classified and pooled.
requirements: Intervention studies must measure outcomes in terms of the distinguished subdomains for effects to be pooled within them
constraints: Applied to preadolescent children aged 6-12 and to intervention studies published between 2000 and April 2017
target_learning_goals: executive functions
attention
academic performance
examples: The review pooled 31 intervention studies and estimated effects separately for acute versus longitudinal designs and for aerobic versus cognitively engaging activity.

The version used had seven playgrounds with 74 problems arrayed easy to difficult, nonlinear free choice of problems, and gold trophies for efficient solutions and silver trophies for other solutions. article_title: The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension∗
citation: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555
title: Segment new social studies textbook text along phrase boundaries to improve children's comprehension
description: The article recommends that written text for elementary social studies be typographically segmented at phrase boundaries — either pausal phrase boundaries (where readers pause reading aloud) or syntactic phrase boundaries (noun phrases, verb phrases, and pattern completers on separate lines) — without changing words or punctuation. The author states: "there is support to recommend that new social studies textbooks that are being written should make some use of the syntactic and pausal phrase formats in presenting the content material." The benefit appears without any prior training for students.
requirements: Passages at or above students' grade level; the study tested passages at or above grade level
constraints: Findings apply only to grades 4 and 7 and to normal students, not special education students; effects on very easy passages and with teacher assistance were not tested
target_learners: elementary school students in grades 4 and 7 of good, average, and poor reading levels
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of social studies textbook content
examples: In the study, 648 grade 4 and 7 students read passages in pausal phrase format (mean line length 5.8 words), syntactic phrase format (mean line length three words), or standard prose format, with comprehension measured by a modified cloze test

article_title: Phonological Processing and Reading and Writing Skills in Literacy
citation: Mendes, G. G., & Barrera, S. D. (2017). Phonological Processing and Reading and Writing Skills in Literacy. Paidéia (Ribeirão Preto), 27(68), 298-305. https://doi.org/10.1590/1982-43272768201707
title: Phonological processing as a multi-component construct underlying literacy
description: The article treats phonological processing as a construct whose cognitive underpinnings are debated, noting that "there is controversy about the cognitive skills underlying this construct." It operationalizes the construct through distinct components — phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming — examined alongside visual processing as predictors of reading and writing. The factor analysis separating these components supports treating them as distinguishable skills rather than a unitary ability.
requirements: The construct is examined through measures of its component skills (phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming) in relation to literacy outcomes.
constraints: The article notes controversy about which cognitive skills underlie the construct.
target_learners: Third-grade elementary school students in early literacy
target_learning_goals: Reading and writing (literacy) performance
examples: The study measured phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming and visual processing in 50 third-grade students and related them to reading and writing performance.
key_sources: Mendes, G. G., & Barrera, S. D. (2017). Phonological Processing and Reading and Writing Skills in Literacy. Paidéia (Ribeirão Preto), 27(68), 298-305. https://doi.org/10.1590/1982-43272768201707

title: Phonological processing assessment battery for third-grade literacy prediction
description: A set of measures of phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming and visual processing administered to 50 students of the 3rd grade of an Elementary Public School to assess their contribution to reading and writing performance. The battery's variables were analyzed correlationally and via exploratory factor analysis, which "suggested the grouping of variables in three factors."

Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09816-3
title: Phantom peer spillover effects: measurement error and selection bias as sources of misleadingly positive compositional effects
description: The article adopts the concept of phantom effects, coined by Harker and Tymms, defined as "misleadingly positive effects of aggregated variables in compositional models — peer spillover effects that are simply an artifact of the inadequacy in the statistical procedures used." Two facets of student-level under-specification produce them: measurement error bias, which can make non-existent compositional effects appear positive and significant, and omitted variable (selection) bias, whose direction depends on correlations among omitted and aggregated variables. The SIMS80 re-analysis empirically illustrates both facets.
requirements: Statistical models accommodating measurement error (e.g., multiple indicators)
Controls for student-level background variables to address selection bias
constraints: The direction of omitted variable bias is not straightforward to predict; the article notes unmeasured confounding positively related to class-average achievement may never be fully resolved in observational studies
target_learning_goals: interpreting compositional (peer) effects in educational research
examples: SIMS80 re-analysis in which positive spillover effects from a linear-in-means model disappeared under doubly latent models with student background controls

title: PHABS-PSS framework: Personal disposition, Health and wellbeing, Acclimation, Background, and Social factors influencing Psychosocial Success
description: The PHABS-PSS framework is the review's organising taxonomy, grouping the 96 identified risk and protective factors into five higher-order domains: "Personal disposition, Health and wellbeing, Acclimation, Background, and Social factors influencing PsychoSocial Success". It was built to reduce the complexity of a disparate literature, make findings conveyable to diverse audiences, and provide "a more practical basis for formulating interventions with real world impact". title: PHelpS peer help system matching ready, willing and able helpers via inspectable user models

citation: Bedard Chloe, St John Laura, Bremer Emily, Graham Jeffrey D., Cairney John. (2019). A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of physically active classrooms on educational and enjoyment outcomes in school age children. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0218633

description: The review defines active classrooms as a teaching technique that "intentionally blends physical activities into core-content academic lessons to satisfy both the learning outcomes of the classroom without sacrificing time spent engaging in PA". description: The review adopts Lubans et al.'s framework of "three broad categories of mechanisms (i.e., neurobiological, psychosocial and behavioural) responsible for the effects of physical activity on cognition". It highlights the behavioural mechanism, proposing that changes in coping and self-regulation skills may improve executive function, and notes on-task behaviour is seen as synonymous with self-regulation in schools. constraints: Not examined in the review itself; mechanisms remain speculative for resistance training in youth

academic achievement
on-task behaviour

title: Phonological processing account of the speech-in-noise–literacy link in younger children
description: The article proposes that the link between speech-in-noise perception and literacy in younger children arises through phonological processing: phonological awareness, phonological memory and phonological recoding are described as processes underpinning both listening in noise and word-level reading. The authors state that "a proposed contribution is through their relationship to the development of phonological processing", citing work indicating speech-in-noise deficits in children with literacy delays reflect shared phonological awareness influence rather than a direct causal relationship. The account is offered as one of several possible auditory, cognitive and linguistic mechanisms.
requirements: The account presumes phonological awareness develops as a critical component of early literacy, integrating speech, language and auditory processing as the article describes
constraints: The article notes speech-in-noise and literacy skills explain only a small amount of variance in literacy outcomes, and that language, vocabulary, working memory and attention were not explored and may influence the association
target_learners: primary school children in the early years of literacy development (Grade 3 age range in this study)
target_learning_goals: literacy development including reading, spelling, writing and grammar/punctuation
examples: The authors contrast Boets and colleagues' conclusion that speech-in-noise deficits in literacy-delayed children are not causal but reflect phonological awareness influence on both tasks, with Vandewalle and Boets' finding of an association beyond phonological processing skills
key_sources: Tomlin D, Bowers P, Zonca B, Graydon K, Phillips J, Rance G. (2025). Speech-in-noise recognition as a predictor of academic achievement. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0324998

article_title: PhacoTrainer: Automatic Artificial Intelligence-Generated Performance Ratings for Cataract Surgery.
citation: Yeh Hsu-Hang, Sen Simmi, Chou Jonathan C., Christopher Karen L., Wang Sophia Y. (2025). PhacoTrainer: Automatic Artificial Intelligence-Generated Performance Ratings for Cataract Surgery. Translational Vision Science & Technology. https://doi.org/10.1167/tvst.14.5.2
title: PhacoTrainer AI metric pipeline for cataract surgical video
description: The pipeline inputs routine cataract surgical videos into a previously developed deep learning segmentation model (YOLACT-based with DarkNet backbone) that detects instrument tips, pupil, and limbus in each frame, from which six metrics are computed: total path length, maximum velocity, covered area, phacoemulsification probe decentration, eye decentration, and zoom level change. The authors write that detecting landmarks “quickly and accurately on entire cataract surgical videos enables the ability to calculate tool-specific artificial intelligence (AI)-derived metrics related to performance.”
requirements: Requires the previously developed and validated deep learning segmentation model and landmark identification algorithm to detect instrument tips and the pupil center in each video frame
constraints: Attending videos were collected from a single center, which may limit the generalizability of the results
The model was not validated in cataract surgeries with complications such as iris prolapse or anterior vitrectomy
Capsulorrhexis performance cannot currently be isolated because the segmentation model does not distinguish very similar-appearing tools such as the cystotome and the hydrodissection cannula
target_learning_goals: cataract surgical skill and instrument-use technique
examples: Ten one-minute clips from attending videos (16,353 labeled frames) were used to validate that pipeline-generated metrics matched metrics from true labeled positions
key_sources: Yeh Hsu-Hang, Sen Simmi, Chou Jonathan C., Christopher Karen L., Wang Sophia Y. (2025). PhacoTrainer: Automatic Artificial Intelligence-Generated Performance Ratings for Cataract Surgery. Translational Vision Science & Technology. https://doi.org/10.1167/tvst.14.5.2

article_title: Image-based and textbook-based virtual reality training on operational skills among junior residents: a proof of concept study.
citation: Lin Wan-Ni, Chuang Hai-Hua, Chao Yi-Ping, Hsin Li-Jen, Kang Chung-Jan, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu, Lee Li-Ang. (2025). Image-based and textbook-based virtual reality training on operational skills among junior residents: a proof of concept study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07245-0
title: Sequence VR surgical training from TBVR foundations to IBVR complexity for novice residents
description: The article recommends a phased approach in which novices begin with semi-immersive textbook-based VR to build foundational knowledge, then progress to immersive image-based VR for complex scenarios. Based on participant feedback, "a phased approach to surgical training may be beneficial: starting with TBVR for establishing foundational knowledge and procedural familiarity and gradually incorporating IBVR". The authors argue this aligns with self-determination theory and lets learners adapt without being overwhelmed.
requirements: Learners should be VR novices or at early expertise levels; modules must be tailored to accommodate learners at different levels of expertise.
constraints: Evidence is a ten-participant proof-of-concept pilot; the authors state future larger-scale studies are necessary to validate these results.
target_learners: Junior residents (R1-R2) new to targeted surgical procedures
target_learning_goals: Preoperative preparation for complex surgeries and performance of basic ORL-HNS procedures
examples: Participants trained with 10-minute VR modules followed by real-patient procedures; the TBVR-IBVR group scored higher in pragmatic quality and hedonic identification during the initial phase.
key_sources: Lin Wan-Ni, Chuang Hai-Hua, Chao Yi-Ping, Hsin Li-Jen, Kang Chung-Jan, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu, Lee Li-Ang. (2025). article_title: Impact of pharmacology perception and learning strategies on academic achievement in undergraduate pharmacy students.
citation: Mengesha Assefa Kebad, Beyna Alemante Tafese, Chanie Gashaw Sisay, Taye Wagaye Atalay, Alemayehu Tekletsadik Tekleslassie, Bizuneh Gizachew Kassahun, Aragie Yonas Sisay, Geremew Gebremariam Wulie, Ayele Habtamu Semagne. (2025). Impact of pharmacology perception and learning strategies on academic achievement in undergraduate pharmacy students. Scientific Reports 15, 16425. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-91510-1
title: Structured questionnaire measuring pharmacology perceptions, learning strategies (SPQ-adapted), and academic achievement
description: A structured, self-administered questionnaire adapted from previously published instruments, including an SPQ-adapted section distinguishing deep learning strategies (e.g., understanding and applying pharmacological concepts) from surface strategies (e.g., memorization for exams), Likert-scale perception items, and self-reported GPA. Psychometric evaluation found "a Cronbach's alpha of 0.85, indicating good internal consistency" and factor loadings from 0.60 to 0.82. It was pilot-tested with 20 students excluded from the main sample.
requirements: Respondents must have completed at least one pharmacology course; first-year students without pharmacology exposure are excluded
constraints: Achievement is self-reported GPA and course grades, which the authors note introduces potential self-report bias
target_learning_goals: assessing perceptions of pharmacology, deep and surface learning strategy use, and academic achievement
examples: Administered to the entire eligible population of 210 students at the University of Gondar between June 1 and August 30, 2024, with trained research assistants providing standardized instructions.

article_title: Development and validation of the Physician's Health Literacy Competence Scale: A step towards effective doctor-patient communication.
citation: Chang C-C, Tseng P-L, Liu C-C, Ming J-L, Fan S-H, Tung C-Y. (2025). Development and validation of the Physician’s Health Literacy Competence Scale: A step towards effective doctor–patient communication. Medicine 104(9): e41643. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000041643
title: Physician’s Health Literacy Competence Scale (PHLCS)
description: The PHLCS is a 20-item self-report instrument assessing physicians’ health literacy competence in clinical interaction scenarios. It was developed through a literature review, expert content validity assessment, and a two-stage cross-sectional refinement with medical students. The article states it comprises "4 factors: building doctor–patient trust, providing a supportive environment, shared decision-making, and verifying medication adherence." Items use Likert agreement and confidence ratings, and the scale is positioned as serving "curriculum development and assessment in medical education."
requirements: Requires respondents who have completed clinical rotations or equivalent clinical experience to rate scenario-based items
constraints: Developed and validated with Taiwanese medical student samples; the authors note the sample "may limit the generalizability of the factor structure"
target_learning_goals: health literacy competence
doctor–patient communication
shared decision-making

citation: Chang C-C, Tseng P-L, Liu C-C, Ming J-L, Fan S-H, Tung C-Y. (2025). Development and validation of the Physician’s Health Literacy Competence Scale: A step towards effective doctor–patient communication. Medicine 104(9): e41643. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000041643
title: Four-dimensional framework of physician health literacy competence
description: The article proposes that physician health literacy competence is a multi-dimensional competency organized around four factors: building doctor–patient trust, providing a supportive environment, shared decision-making, and verifying medication adherence. It positions the framework as extending patient-focused models: "The PHLCS extends these models by evaluating physicians’ competencies in fostering trust, supporting SDM, and ensuring treatment adherence." The four factors correlate highly and are modeled as a single latent higher-order factor. Earlier development identified five dimensions and 16 subdimensions with 27 indicators before factor refinement.
requirements: Physician–patient interaction scenarios as the item context for assessing the four dimensions
constraints: Grounded in Taiwanese medical education contexts; the authors note cultural communication norms may affect the scale’s effectiveness elsewhere
target_learning_goals: patient-centered care
health literacy competence

article_title: Design and evaluation of a problem-based learning VR module for apparel fit correction training.
citation: Galada, Aditi and Baytar, Fatma. (2025). Design and evaluation of a problem-based learning VR module for apparel fit correction training. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311587
title: Expose learners to physical garment development and fitting sessions before introducing digital PBL garment-simulation modules
description: The article recommends sequencing physical fitting experience ahead of digital problem-based learning with garment simulations, because prior apparel spatial visualization skill predicted larger fit-correction gains. The authors write that "participants should first be exposed to physical garment development and fitting sessions before being introduced to the digital problem-based learning module," interpreting spatial skill as a prerequisite for learning efficiently from digital simulations. Interview feedback that prior physical-garment experience was needed supported this recommendation.
requirements: Learners need prior apparel spatial visualization skill, developed through physical garment development and fitting experience, before the digital module
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in a single small one-group pretest-posttest study with college students and limited demographic diversity
target_learning_goals: Fit correction skills
Apparel spatial visualization skills
examples: In the study, participants completed a pre-test of apparel spatial visualization before training, and regression showed the ASVT pre-test score significantly predicted the increase in FCST score
key_sources: Galada, Aditi and Baytar, Fatma. (2025). Design and evaluation of a problem-based learning VR module for apparel fit correction training. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311587

article_title: "Pharmacotrophy": a playful tournament for game- and team-based learning in pharmacology education - assessing its impact on students' performance.
citation: Delage Clément, Palayer Maeva, Lerouet Dominique, Besson Valérie C. (2024). “Pharmacotrophy”: a playful tournament for game- and team-based learning in pharmacology education - assessing its impact on students’ performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05157-z
title: Pharmacotrophy: a two-week game-, team- and competition-based pharmacology tournament using Kahoot! quizzes
description: Pharmacotrophy is a team tournament in which teams of three 4th- or 5th-year pharmacy students compete by answering pharmacology questions via live online quizzes (Kahoot!) and face-to-face matches, over a two-week period during exam revision. As the article states, it “involved a combination of remote matches using the online quiz creation tool Kahoot!® and in-person matches”, with group and knockout stages leading to a final. Teachers wrote and curated questions from the pharmacology curriculum, and correct answers were given without explanations to encourage self-directed revision.
requirements: Teams of three students formed and registered themselves; questions had to be answerable swiftly, automatically scoreable, and compatible with Kahoot!
constraints: The competition was not open to 1st–3rd year students because questions could cover material they had not yet studied; teachers invested an estimated 36–54 hours each over the 9 days of competition.
target_learning_goals: revision of the full pharmacology curriculum
motivation to revise before exams
examples: In 2021 the entire tournament was run remotely due to lockdown; in 2022 group matches and quarter-finals were remote and semi-finals and final were face-to-face.

article_title: Role of peer learning and self-efficacy in parasympathetic activity during the simulation learning process in nursing students.
citation: Nakayama, N., Ejiri, H., Arakawa, N., & Makino, T. (2023). Role of peer learning and self‐efficacy in parasympathetic activity during the simulation learning process in nursing students. Nursing Open, 10, 552–559. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1321
title: Phased peer‐learning simulation cycle alternating individual patient observation with peer discussion
description: The article's simulation ran as a repeating cycle in which students first assess a high‐fidelity manikin patient individually, then share findings with peers, then re‐observe individually to collect missing information, followed by reflection and peer summarizing phases. The authors state "Scene 1 contained 5 phases", beginning when "the participants observed the patients individually (5 min)" and then "shared information with their peers (5 min)"; Scene 2 repeated this structure in four phases.
requirements: Students work through the phases in small peer groups, as in the study where "One group consisted of four to six people."
constraints: Peer groups were not organized in advance by self‐efficacy level, so "the influence of the self‐efficacy of the group members could not be considered."
target_learning_goals: patient assessment during simulation
managing stress during simulation learning
examples: Participants assessed a stable postoperative patient in Scene 1 and the same patient with intra‐abdominal bleeding in Scene 2, moving through observation, peer sharing, re‐observation, reflection and summarizing phases.

article_title: Anatomic accuracy, physiologic characteristics, and fidelity of very low birth weight infant airway simulators.
citation: Lengua Hinojosa Patricia, Eifinger Frank, Wagner Michael, Herrmann Jochen, Wolf Monika, Ebenebe Chinedu Ulrich, von der Wense Axel, Jung Philipp, Mai Aram, Bohnhorst Bettina, Longardt Ann Carolin, Hillebrand Georg, Schmidtke Susanne, Guthmann Florian, Aderhold Martina, Schwake Ida, Sprinz Maria, Singer Dominique, Deindl Philipp. (2022). Anatomic accuracy, physiologic characteristics, and fidelity of very low birth weight infant airway simulators. Pediatric Research 92(3):783-790. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-021-01823-w
title: Two-dimensional fidelity framework for medical simulators: physical fidelity and functional fidelity
description: The article describes simulator fidelity, defined as the degree of exactness with which something is reproduced, as having two dimensions. It states that "Physical fidelity reflects the quality of the simulator to imitate physical characteristics like haptic and optical impressions" while "Functional fidelity describes the simulator's ability to demonstrate complex scenarios". The study operationalizes both dimensions in its expert rating protocol: experts rated skin, face, mouth, gingiva, tongue, glottis, vocal cords, airway, and anatomy after visual inspection, then performed airway maneuvers and rated functional fidelity. The article cites Curtis et al. for the claim that high physical fidelity is crucial for developing psychomotor skills and functional fidelity for building cognitive comprehension.
requirements: Expert raters with relevant clinical expertise to evaluate both fidelity dimensions
High-resolution airway imagery and the ability to perform airway maneuvers on the simulator for functional assessment
constraints: The framework is attributed to prior literature (Curtis et al. and others) cited by the article, not developed by this study
target_learning_goals: airway management of very low birth weight infants
bag-mask ventilation
endotracheal intubation
less-invasive surfactant administration
examples: Experts rated physical fidelity from video-laryngoscope photographs of mouth, pharynx, epiglottis, and glottis, and functional fidelity after performing bag-mask ventilation, oral intubation, nasal intubation, and LISA on each simulator in randomized order

article_title: The development and use of a pharmacist-specific Mini-CEX for postgraduate year trainees in Taiwan.
citation: Wei Chung-Jen, Lu Tzu-Hsuan, Chien Shu-Chen, Huang Wan-Tsui, Liu Yueh-Ping, Chan Cho-Yu, Chiu Chiung-Hsuan. (2019). The development and use of a pharmacist-specific Mini-CEX for postgraduate year trainees in Taiwan. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1602-2
title: Pharmacist-specific Chinese-language Mini-CEX instrument with nine competency domains
description: A workplace-based assessment form adapted from the physician Mini-CEX for Taiwanese PGY pharmacy trainees, covering "pharmacology knowledge, patient care knowledge, consultation skills, professional health education skills, management of drug distribution, organization and efficiency, professionalism, communication skills, and overall performance". Each competency is rated on a 1–9 scale banded as unsatisfactory (1–3), satisfactory (4–6), or excellent (7–9), benchmarked to a TSHSP stage 3 competent pharmacist. Descriptive items were adapted from ASHP guidelines, translated into Chinese, and validated via a two-round Delphi process with five experts.
requirements: Evaluator workshops prior to use to establish consensus and rating consistency
Evaluators with senior pharmacist status, at least four years of teaching-hospital experience, and instructor certification
constraints: Developed for Taiwan's PGY context, where new pharmacists perform basic tasks such as dispensing and consultation; the article states direct application of the physician Mini-CEX to pharmacists is inappropriate
target_learners: Postgraduate-year pharmacy trainees in teaching hospitals
target_learning_goals: Core pharmacist clinical competencies including patient care, consultation, communication, and organization and efficiency
examples: Used in a main study in which two evaluators (a direct supervisor and a mentor) each observed a trainee dispensing medication, providing clinical pharmacy services, or giving a medication consultation, then completed the form
